faq.a: Neisseria relies on the MAC to be lysed; loss of late‑component proteins prevents bacterial killing, allowing rapid bloodstream invasion.
faq.q: Why do complement deficiencies predispose specifically to meningococcal infection?

faq.a: No; a normal CH50 can mask a functional defect of a single late component if other proteins compensate. Specific component assays are needed.
faq.q: Can a normal CH50 rule out complement deficiency?

faq.a: Yes; it reduces the bacterial load that the complement system must clear, markedly lowering sepsis risk.
faq.q: Is vaccination effective in patients with complement deficiency?

exam: A 7‑year‑old boy from rural Kenya presents with fever, petechial rash and hypotension. What is the most urgent next step? — Give empiric ceftriaxone immediately and draw blood for culture; delay for complement testing would be fatal.

How does a low CH50 help you differentiate between early‑ vs late‑component deficiency? — Low CH50 indicates a quantitative problem in any component; you then use AH50 and specific assays to locate early vs late deficiency.

A patient with known properdin deficiency develops meningococcal sepsis despite vaccination. Which additional preventive measure is indicated? — Provide prophylactic penicillin until vaccination schedule is updated and educate on early presentation.
Why is eculizumab contraindicated in a patient with recurrent meningococcal infections? — Eculizumab blocks C5, reproducing a late‑component deficiency and dramatically raises meningococcal risk.

During a malaria outbreak, a child shows low C3 and haemolysis. How do you decide if this is complement deficiency or malaria‑related consumption? — Correlate with malaria smear; if parasites are present, consumption is likely; otherwise pursue CH50 and specific assays.

What distinguishes complement‑mediated autoimmune haemolysis from warm IgG AIHA on laboratory testing? — Complement‑mediated haemolysis shows low C3/C4 and a positive direct Coombs for C3 only, whereas warm AIHA is Coombs positive for IgG with normal complement.
A patient with recurrent meningococcal sepsis has normal C3 and C4 but low CH50. Which component is most likely missing? — One of the terminal components (C5‑C9) because early components are normal.

In a low‑resource hospital without CH50 testing, what clinical clue would prompt you to start complement replacement therapy? — Recurrent meningococcal sepsis with documented low complement activity on prior testing or strong family history of similar infections.
ai.title: Complement System in Clinical Practice
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: The complement cascade links antibodies and innate immunity, driving opsonisation, inflammation and cell lysis. Deficiencies predispose to severe bacterial infections, especially meningococcaemia, and can mimic autoimmune haemolysis.

b: Classical pathway – triggered by IgG/IgM immune complexes
Lectin pathway – triggered by mannose‑binding lectin on microbes
Alternative pathway – spontaneous tick‑over, amplified on bacterial surfaces
sections.p: Complement is a group of plasma proteins (C1‑C9) that, once activated, amplify inflammation, tag microbes for phagocytosis and form the membrane‑attack complex (MAC) to lyse cells.

b: Early‑component (C1‑C4) deficiency – predisposes to immune‑complex disease (lupus‑like) and severe bacterial sepsis
Late‑component (C5‑C9) deficiency – classic recurrent meningococcal or gonococcal sepsis
sections.p: Clinical severity is judged by the extent of infection and organ damage rather than a numeric stage; however, complement‑mediated diseases are grouped by component deficiency (early vs late) because they predict infection risk.

b: Inherited deficiency of C5‑C8 (autosomal recessive) – most common cause of recurrent meningococcal disease in African children
Properdin deficiency (X‑linked) – severe meningococcaemia, often in young males
Acquired consumption in severe sepsis, malaria, or disseminated intravascular coagulation
Auto‑antibodies against C1q in systemic lupus erythematosus
HIV‑related complement consumption
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, acquired and inherited causes must be considered together.

b: Fever, rigors, petechial rash, hypotension – classic meningococcal sepsis
Unexplained haemolysis, dark urine, jaundice – complement‑mediated autoimmune haemolysis
Recurrent infections after routine vaccinations (e.g., pneumococcal) suggest late‑component loss
sections.p: Patients with complement deficiency usually present with recurrent, rapidly progressive bacterial sepsis, especially meningococcaemia, or with atypical haemolytic anaemia when immune complexes are involved.
When CH50 or component assays are unavailable, rely on clinical pattern (recurrent meningococcal sepsis) and treat empirically.

t.b: Is overall complement activity sufficient? Low CH50 indicates a quantitative deficiency of any component; normal CH50 with low specific component suggests functional defect.
Is the alternative pathway intact? Low AH50 with normal CH50 points to early‑pathway deficiency.

t.a: Specific component quantification (C3, C4, C5‑C9, properdin)
t.b: Which protein is missing? Low levels confirm the deficient component; normal levels rule it out.
Is haemolysis immune mediated? Positive Coombs with low complement suggests complement‑mediated autoimmune haemolysis.

t.a: Culture of blood/CSF during acute sepsis
t.b: What organism is causing the infection? Neisseria meningitidis or gonorrhoeae are classic in late‑component deficiency.
Is the deficiency inherited? Confirms diagnosis and guides family counselling.

b: Persistent hypotension despite fluids
Rapidly falling platelet count and rising INR
New neurological deficits suggesting meningitis
sections.p: Uncontrolled complement deficiency can rapidly progress to septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and multi‑organ failure.

b: Empiric third‑generation cephalosporin (e.g., ceftriaxone) for suspected meningococcaemia – covers Neisseria, safe in most comorbidities
If meningococcal disease confirmed, give high‑dose intravenous penicillin G if susceptible
Vaccinate against Neisseria meningitidis (serogroups A, C, W, Y, and locally prevalent serogroup X) and pneumococcus – essential secondary prevention
Consider plasma‑derived complement replacement (e.g., fresh frozen plasma) in acute severe deficiency when specific concentrates unavailable
Avoid drugs that further impair complement (e.g., eculizumab) unless indicated for another condition
sections.p: Treat the infection urgently, then address the underlying complement defect.

b: Annual meningococcal booster and pneumococcal vaccination
Educate families to seek immediate care for fever with rash or rapid deterioration
Screen siblings for inherited deficiency if a genetic cause is identified
sections.p: Long‑term care focuses on infection prophylaxis and monitoring for autoimmune complications.

b: Asplenia – also predisposes to encapsulated bacteria but lacks complement‑specific lab pattern
Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (warm IgG) – positive Coombs but normal complement levels
Severe malaria – can consume complement but presents with parasitaemia
sections.p: Conditions that also cause recurrent sepsis or haemolysis.

b: CH50 may be normal in early infection despite low C5‑C9 because acute‑phase reactants raise total protein
Low C3 alone can reflect consumption in infection rather than genetic deficiency
False‑negative cultures after prior antibiotics can mask the causative organism

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly progressive fever with petechial rash or purpura
Signs of septic shock (BP <90/60 mmHg, altered mental status)
New onset severe anaemia with jaundice and dark urine
